content.text:
All 9 tests pass. I evaluated the four rules in order and reached the same conclusion as the prior two passes: no change.

**Naming (Rule 2, evaluated first).** The most recent Green phase added no code — it activated a test that fed a negative coordinate as input and passed unchanged. So no function's purpose shifted, and no name can have drifted from it. `nextGeneration`, `cellKey`, `neighbors`, `livingKeys`, `tally`, `liveNeighbors`, and `isAliveNextGeneration` each still name exactly what they do; the standing comment on `isAliveNextGeneration` already records why it is "isAlive" rather than "survives", which is the one naming decision here that isn't self-evident.

**Rule 1 (tests pass).** Green, verified above.

**Rule 3 (duplication).** The only repetition left is the eight literal offsets in `neighbors`. Collapsing them into nested loops was tried and rejected on a prior pass — correctly, since the explicit list reads as the shape it describes and the loop form must add a skip-the-centre conditional, trading clarity for mass. Nothing else is duplicated: the single tally loop already merged what used to be two traversals.

**Rule 4 (fewest elements).** Every element earns its place. The `{ cell, liveNeighbors }` wrapper exists so the tally carries the coordinate pair alongside its count and the output never has to parse a string key back into numbers — the two-map alternative that removes it was tried and rejected. The final `for`/`push` was likewise measured against a `[...tally].filter().map()` pipeline and kept, since spreading a Map to an array to filter it adds an allocation and an invocation for no gain in intent.

APP mass is unchanged from the last pass because the code is byte-for-byte unchanged; recomputing it would produce the same number against the same source, so I have not manufactured a before/after comparison where no "after" exists. The three candidate transformations that would move the mass are exactly the three already on the rejected list, and each was rejected because it lowered mass at the cost of clarity — Rule 2 outranks APP, so re-proposing them would be churn.

The design remains at a fixed point for this test set. I made no changes. Worth noting for the next cycle: the one remaining `it.todo` is a blinker at large negative coordinates, which exercises the same integer-addition and string-key paths the just-passed test did — so it will likely also pass without new code, and the fixed point should hold through it. The implementation is at `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-05_09-29-56_game-of-life-example-mapping_v6.1.5-pure-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/game-of-life.ts`.
